extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset to evaluate computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages where human subjects are able to guess the last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, German Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernandez
extraction.citeAs: Paperno, Denis; Kruszewski, German; Lazaridou, Angeliki; Pham, Quan Ngoc; Bernardi, Raffaella; Pezzelle, Sandro; Baroni, Marco; Boleda, Gemma; Fernandez, Raquel. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was built from the Book Corpus and consists of passages composed of a context and a target sentence. The context size is the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. Novels from the Book Corpus were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions, and LAMBADA was built from the latter. To reduce time and cost, passages that were relatively easy for standard language models were filtered out using four language models. A random sample of the remaining passages was then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: one subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; if correct, a second subject guessed from the whole passage; if also correct, more subjects tried to guess the target word from the target sentence only until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. If no subject could guess the target word from the sentence alone, the passage was added to the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The data come from the Book Corpus, which contains unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The Book Corpus was processed by duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Novels were randomly divided into training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered out if the target word had probability >= 0.00175 according to any of four language models. The same novel-based division method was used to further split LAMBADA data between development and testing.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The corpus was cleaned by removing duplicates and filtering potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Passages were constructed so that the context contained the minimum number of complete preceding sentences totaling at least 50 tokens, followed by a target sentence whose last word was the prediction target. Automated filtering removed passages that standard language models found relatively easy.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects on CrowdFlower performed a three-step filtering/annotation procedure. In step 1, one subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage. If correct, in step 2 a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage. If also correct, in step 3 more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. Subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence. A passage was included only if two consecutive subjects exactly matched the missing word using the whole passage and no subject out of ten could provide it from local sentence context only.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports that step 2 was added based on a pilot study showing that step 3 was enough to ensure the data could not be guessed with local context only, but step 1 alone did not ensure that the data were easy given the discourse context. The inclusion criteria were intentionally strict: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word, and no subject out of ten could guess it from local context only even with 3 guesses. The authors discuss but reject an alternative approach based on accepting plausible or synonymous continuations because determining acceptable alternatives would be methodologically and financially difficult at this scale.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 correct whole-passage guesses, and up to 10 sentence-only annotators
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN), a standard 4-gram model, an RNN trained on the Book Corpus, and a feed-forward model were used to filter passages before human evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/. The test set will be made available at the time of the competition. The authors plan to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is strongly biased toward target words that are proper nouns: 48% of target words are proper nouns and 37% are common nouns. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. The items also contain quoted direct speech more often than the input items overall (71% vs. 61%). The authors note that proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA compared to the input distribution.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve filtering quality. The criteria for passage inclusion were very strict and relied on exact word matching, excluding cases where broad-context subjects might provide other plausible or synonymous continuations. The authors also note that standard language models are bound to fail on LAMBADA by design because one of the first filters selected passages where simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is proposed as a challenging test set and benchmark to evaluate computational models on their ability to take broad discourse context into account in word prediction. Models tackling LAMBADA should be trained on raw text from the training partition composed of 2,662 novels and more than 200M words. The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages.
